section_practice.guidance: Span of control refers to the number of subordinates (employees) that a manager is directly responsible for (1 mark). A wide span of control means a manager oversees many employees (1 mark), while a narrow span means fewer direct reports (1 mark). The appropriate span depends on factors such as the complexity of the work, the skill level of employees, and the management style used (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Define the term 'span of control'. (4 marks)

steps: Taylor argued workers are motivated by money — piece-rate pay increases output but ignores non-financial needs.
Maslow's hierarchy suggests escalating needs: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation.
Herzberg distinguished hygiene factors (pay, conditions — prevent dissatisfaction) from motivators (achievement, responsibility — create satisfaction).
Modern firms combine financial incentives (bonuses, profit-sharing) with non-financial motivators (training, empowerment, recognition).
chains.title: Motivation theories explain what drives performance
chains.result: Effective motivation combines financial rewards with meaningful work, recognition and development opportunities.

steps: Autocratic leaders decide without consultation — fast but can reduce morale and creativity.
Democratic leaders involve employees — improving motivation and ideas but slowing decisions.
Laissez-faire leaders delegate extensively — effective with skilled teams but risks confusion without direction.
The most effective style depends on context: crisis favours autocratic, creative projects favour democratic.
chains.title: Leadership style affects employee engagement
chains.result: No single leadership style is best — effective leaders adapt their approach to the situation and team.

steps: Tall structures have many hierarchy layers — clear command chains but slow communication and high overheads.
Flat structures have few layers — faster communication and more autonomy but wider spans of control.
Centralised structures keep decisions at the top — ensuring consistency but reducing local responsiveness.
Decentralised structures push decisions down — increasing speed and empowerment but risking inconsistency.
chains.title: Organisational structure shapes communication and control
chains.result: Structure involves trade-offs between control and flexibility — the best fit depends on business size and strategy.

steps: Motivated, well-led employees in an appropriate structure are more productive — more output per hour.
Higher productivity reduces unit labour costs, improving competitiveness and profit margins.
Investment in training develops skills, enabling workers to handle higher-value tasks and adapt to change.
Low staff turnover reduces recruitment costs and preserves institutional knowledge.
chains.title: Effective people management raises productivity
chains.result: People management is a key source of competitive advantage — engaged employees drive productivity, quality and innovation.

evaluation.title: Motivation theories are culturally biased
evaluation.content: Maslow and Herzberg developed theories in Western contexts. In different cultures, social belonging or security may outweigh self-actualisation. Effective motivation requires understanding the specific workforce context.

evaluation.title: Flexible working has trade-offs
evaluation.content: Remote work and flexitime improve work-life balance but can weaken team cohesion and make supervision harder. Not all roles suit flexibility, creating potential inequity within the workforce.

evaluation.title: Training investment carries poaching risk
evaluation.content: Firms that invest heavily in training risk losing skilled workers to competitors offering higher wages. This discourages investment in transferable skills. But firms that don't train risk falling behind technologically.

section_common_mistakes.title: Confusing Dismissal and Redundancy
section_common_mistakes.examTip: In exam answers, clearly state whether the scenario involves dismissal (individual's fault) or redundancy (role eliminated). This distinction is worth marks.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Students use dismissal and redundancy interchangeably or mix up which relates to the individual vs the role.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Dismissal is about the individual (misconduct, poor performance). Redundancy is about the role (no longer needed due to restructuring, automation, or declining demand). Redundancy entitles the employee to redundancy pay.

section_common_mistakes.title: Oversimplifying Motivation Theories
section_common_mistakes.examTip: For high marks, name the theory, explain it briefly, apply it to the context, and evaluate its limitations. Use the structure: theory → application → evaluation.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Students just list the theory without applying it to the business context or evaluating its limitations.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always apply the theory to the specific scenario. For example, don't just describe Maslow's hierarchy — explain which level is relevant and how the business could address that need. Then evaluate: Maslow's hierarchy may not apply in all cultures and assumes needs are met sequentially.

section_common_mistakes.title: Thinking Flat Structures Are Always Better
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Always evaluate both tall and flat structures. Consider the business's size, industry, and culture when recommending a structure.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Students assume flat organisational structures are superior because they enable faster communication.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Flat structures can overload managers (too-wide spans of control), create confusion about authority, and make career progression less clear. Tall structures suit large, complex organisations that need clear reporting lines and close supervision.

section_common_mistakes.title: Confusing Herzberg's Two Factors
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Remember: hygiene factors are like the foundation — they must be adequate, but building higher motivation requires motivators. Use this distinction clearly in your answers.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Students claim that improving hygiene factors (like pay) will motivate workers.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Herzberg argued that hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfaction — they do not create motivation. Improving pay removes the source of complaint but does not make workers enthusiastic. Only motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility) create genuine satisfaction and motivation.

section_common_mistakes.title: Not Linking Leadership Style to Context
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Always justify your recommended leadership style with reference to the specific context. Use phrases like 'in this situation... because...' to show contextual awareness.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Students state that one leadership style (usually democratic) is the best without considering the situation.
section_common_mistakes.correction: The most effective leadership style depends on the context — the nature of the task, the skills of the workforce, the time available, and the business culture. Autocratic leadership may be best in a crisis; democratic works well with skilled, experienced teams.
